themes.title: One Nation & the party system
themes.dek: The surge itself: who is moving to One Nation, what pulls them, what holds them back, and how the majors are being reshaped around it.

themes.title: Cost of living & the economy
themes.dek: Household finances, interest rates, energy prices and the people respondents say are responsible for them.

themes.title: The budget, tax & housing
themes.dek: The May budget and its housing-tax package: awareness, verdicts, and what voters would rather the money went to.

themes.title: Immigration & multiculturalism
themes.dek: The issue the cycle most visibly turned on, asked outright: levels, source countries, and whether diversity still serves the country.

themes.title: The national mood
themes.dek: Right direction or wrong track, the system's legitimacy, pride in the country, and what the country was actually talking about each month.

themes.title: Security, energy & the wider world
themes.dek: Bondi, the Iran war, fuel security and where voters locate the safe ground between defence and net zero.

themes.title: Issues, leaders & policy
themes.dek: Which issues matter, which party is trusted on them, and the policy one-offs that fit nowhere else.

entries.question: Thinking about overall immigration to Australia, including total number of people leaving and arriving, do you think we need…

rows: Immigration levels to stay about the same

prose: Their message on immigration being too high appears to be paying dividends, with only 8 per cent of voting age Australians saying immigration should be higher and 28 per cent that it is about right, compared to 64 per cent saying our immigration are levels are too high. Forty three per cent want a big decrease in immigration.
Only 8 per cent of voters think Australia’s immigration levels need to be higher, compared to 64% who want a decrease. Tellingly, 43 per cent want a big decrease.

entries.question: Do you support the government's social media ban for under-16s? (tracked pre/post implementation)
prose: There was strong support however for the government’s social media ban on under 16s.

Sky News asked voters whether they supported the ban before its implementation and after, and the support has only strengthened, with strongly support at 40 per cent (up 3 per cent) and somewhat support 29 per cent (steady) combining to show 69 per cent of voters support the ban, compared to only 16 per cent who don’t support it.

entries.question: How well has Prime Minister Anthony Albanese responded to the Bondi terror attack?
options: As well as can be expected given the circumstances
prose: The Prime Minister had his own reality check, with only 5 per cent of voters saying he responded very well to the Bondi terror attack, compared to 28 per cent who said he has done very badly.
He can take some comfort in 38 per cent of respondents saying he did as well as can be expected given in the circumstances.

entries.question: Current voting intention of 2025 Liberal voters (2025 vote recall × current VI)
prose: The Liberals and Nationals were down across the board compared to 2025, with primary vote for the Liberals at 14 per cent (-6.7 per cent), LNP at 4 per cent (-3.1 per cent) and Nationals at 2 per cent (-1.8 per cent).

It’s no surprise where One Nation would pick up seats, with the party outpolling the combined Liberals and Nationals in outer metropolitan seats 27 per cent to 20 per cent, and in rural seats 35 per cent to 21 per cent.

entries.question: Thinking about the next election, who do you think the best person would be to lead the Liberal party to give it the best chance of forming government?
Is the government responsible for the February 2026 interest-rate rise? (partly/wholly vs not)
prose: And two-thirds of voters think Labor is either partly or wholly responsible for last week’s rate hike.

entries.question: Would you ever support One Nation?
prose: It’s tempting to say One Nation’s vote could have peaked given it is down from 28 per cent to 24 per cent, but the party certainly has a higher ceiling; we asked voters if they would ever support the minor party, and 48 per cent said yes.

prose: Sky News will be regularly checking in on the main issues for voters – and our first analysis has cost of living way out in front at 41 per cent, with the next highest being immigration and housing affordability at 10 per cent each.

Labor has a slim lead as the best party to handle cost of living on 25 per cent, the Coalition next best on 22 per cent, and One Nation lagging on 13 per cent, but more rate rises could shift that dial significantly.

entries.question: What do you expect energy prices to do over the next 12 months?
prose: Thirty-nine per cent expect them to “increase a lot” and a further 38 per cent expect them to “increase somewhat”.
The data showed 63 per cent of the public believed joblessness would increase further, while one in five believed unemployment would “increase a lot”.
Just six per cent expected the cost of energy to decrease.
“Working class” respondents held the bleakest views, with 45 per cent expecting fuel to increase “a lot”.

entries.question: Have you taken action to reduce your fuel consumption?
prose: Just under half of those polled said they had taken action to reduce fuel consumption as a result of widespread price jumps in Australia.

entries.question: What do you expect unemployment to do over the next year?
prose: The data showed 63 per cent of the public believed joblessness would increase further, while one in five believed unemployment would “increase a lot”.
Just six per cent believed unemployment could fall.

entries.question: How do you rate Donald Trump's handling of the war in Iran?
prose: More than half of all voters thought Mr Trump was handling his war in Iran “very badly”, as a total of 71 per cent of respondents thought he was doing poorly.
Sixty-six per cent said Mr Trump was handling the conflict badly.

entries.question: Which party is best equipped to handle the economy and government debt / security and defence / immigration (battery repeat)
prose: The Coalition was seen as better at handling the economy and government debt (31 per cent) and security and defence (28 per cent).
One Nation dominated on immigration, with 36 per cent of voters rating it the party best equipped to handle the issue.

entries.question: Do you think the Liberal National Coalition and One Nation should team up to try form government?
prose: Forty-six per cent of all voters said the Liberal-National Coalition and One Nation should team up to form government.
Fifty-three per cent of people intending to vote One Nation wanted cooperation, as well as 45 per cent Coalition voters, yet only 20 per cent of Labor voters supported the move.

entries.question: The May Federal Budget includes changes to negative gearing on investment properties, capital gains taxes, and extended the ban on foreign buyers purchasing established homes. Do you think these changes will increase or reduce rents? (significantly increase → significantly reduce, not sure)
entries.note: Public verdict on the housing-tax package's rent effect: 48% expect rents to INCREASE vs 12% who expect a fall (net +36). Coalition politicians' attack line works on their base (net increase 55-67 among LNP cohorts) but Labor voters believe their own policy (+13). Renters themselves: net +22 expect increases.

entries.question: On Tuesday, 12 May 2026 the Australian Federal Government handed down the 2026–27 Federal Budget. How much, if anything, have you seen, read or heard about this?; then of those who had heard anything: Overall, how good or bad do you think the budget will be… for the country as a whole / for you personally
entries.note: Second read of the budget module, five months on. Awareness faded (net +30 → -10) but the verdict hardened: those still paying attention are the most hostile (attention-level table: net good -69 among 'a great deal'). Among One Nation voters the country rating is net -78. September N=868 perceptions base.
